title: Deterministic Output Seals and Offline Tool Sync PRD
body:
Purpose
This doc proposes a combined server+SDK mechanism—Deterministic Output Seals (DOS) and Offline Tool Sync (OTS)—to support low-bandwidth/unstable-client scenarios while preserving atomic tool-call semantics and reproducible structured outputs from the Hosted API. The goal is to make progressive streaming useful to clients that need reliable replays, local previews, and offline retries without sacrificing server-side correctness or telemetry visibility.

Problem statement
Many customers embed Redwood-hosted streaming responses into mobile, edge, and third-party integrations where connectivity is intermittent. Current streaming semantics optimize for low-latency incremental delivery but leave ambiguous boundaries for tool invocations and structured output commits when clients disconnect or retry. Consequences:
- Duplicate or partial tool execution when clients reconnect and re-issue requests.
- Inconsistent state for consumers that need deterministic JSON outputs for downstream processing (tickets, database writes).
- Poor developer ergonomics: SDKs try ad-hoc buffering, leading to complex client logic and fragile behavior.

Principles and constraints
- Determinism: given the same request and sealed events, a replay should produce the same committed outputs and tool-call log.
- Minimal server-side state: avoid long-lived per-client session state unless explicitly reserved (Dedicated customers can opt for sticky sessions).
- Graceful streaming: incremental partial text/frames are still streamed, but commits are explicit and durable.
- Client-friendly SDK: hide complexity (replay, resume, idempotency) behind a small surface area for most developers.
- Observability: every seal and tool execution must be traceable with token-level cost and duration attached.

High-level proposal
1) Deterministic Output Seals (DOS): a compact, server-calculated commitment token emitted during streaming that denotes a stable prefix/state of the response. The DOS is a cryptographic digest over canonicalized output frames + tool-call intents up to that point and includes a monotonic sequence number.
2) Offline Tool Sync (OTS): a companion lightweight mechanism for queuing and reconciling tool invocations initiated by the model. Tool calls are recorded as surrogate events on the server with an idempotency key derived from the DOS + tool-index. Clients can request an OTS reconciliation snapshot on reconnect to learn which tool calls completed, which were attempted, and the final structured outputs tied to each DOS.
3) SDK ergonomics: SDKs expose resume() and reconcile() helpers that accept a DOS token and a local incremental transcript. The SDK will:
   - Accept streamed frames and buffer them into a canonical transcript.
   - Surface "seal" events to application callbacks when DOS tokens arrive.
   - Persist minimal metadata (last_seen_dos, last_tool_index) in local storage for offline app restarts.
   - On reconnect, call reconcile(dos) to fetch authoritative decisions and apply locally.

Why this is different from naive checkpoints
Existing partial-response patterns stream text but don't provide a compact, verifiable commitment that downstream systems can rely on without re-running completions. DOS provides:
- A digest that a client can use to verify a replayed transcript (helps for security-sensitive flows).
- A stable mapping between a seal and the set of tool calls and structured output edges observed at that point.

API surface (sketch)
- /v1/responses (POST) standard streaming generation request; the server will optionally include "seal" frame events in the stream payloads when a DOS boundary is reached.
- /v1/responses/{response_id}/reconcile?dos={dos_token} (GET) returns the canonical structured output bundle and tool-call ledger for that DOS. This endpoint is cheap (read-only snapshot) and can be served from read replicas.
- Tool-call receipts are available at /v1/tool-calls/{call_id} (GET) and include status, result, associated dos_token, and idempotency_key.

Streaming frame envelope (example fields; text description only)
- frame_id: monotonic per-response integer
- type: {partial_text, seal, tool_call_intent, tool_call_result, structured_fragment}
- payload: text or JSON blob (clients treat partial_text as display-only until sealed)
- dos_token: present on seal frames, opaque string
- signature: optional HMAC when customer requires signed seals (enterprise feature)

Behavioral guarantees
- After a DOS seal is emitted, the server guarantees the set of tool-call intents and structured fragments that are associated with that DOS will not be retroactively changed. Later DOS tokens may extend or update structured outputs via explicit merge semantics, but previous DOS tokens remain stable snapshots.
- Tool calls initiated before a DOS might be in-flight; their definitive success/failure will be visible via OTS reconciliation.
- Replaying a request with identical inputs and model-version should yield DOS tokens that map to the same snapshot; if the server cannot guarantee that (e.g., nondeterministic model stochasticity), reconcile will return a special code indicating non-reproducible result and provide the best-effort snapshot and provenance.

Tool-call semantics and idempotency
- Each model-initiated tool_call_intent frame contains a suggested idempotency_key: sha256(dos_token + ":" + local_tool_index). The server stores a short-lived record (TTL 72 hours for hosted API) mapping idempotency_key -> tool result.
- If a client reconnects and replays frames that cause the same intent key, the server will surface the recorded result instead of re-invoking the integration (when integrations support idempotency).
- For integrations that cannot be deduplicated, the server will mark the tool-call as "replayed_possible_duplicate" and include metadata to help clients reconcile (timestamps, upstream event ids).

Offline-first client patterns (SDK guide)
- Local display: render partial_text frames immediately for UX, but tag them as transient. Attach the latest dos_token when available to the UI state.
- Durable local state: persist last_seen_dos, last_tool_index, and the incremental transcript. Keep only the minimum needed to reconcile later (avoid storing large cached models).
- Reconnect flow: on network return, SDK calls reconcile(last_seen_dos). If reconcile indicates missing tool results, SDK will fetch the tool-call ledger and synthesize any missing results into the transcript, emitting events for app handlers to apply database writes or user notifications.
- Offline retries: SDK exposes safe_resend() that will attempt to replay user actions that led to a response; uses dos_token to derive idempotency keys automatically. App developers are encouraged to treat reconcile() as the authority for committing side effects server-side.

Developer-facing examples (conceptual)
- Chat app on mobile: show streaming tokens as they arrive. When a DOS arrives, mark message as "committed" in UI and enable downstream webhooks to receive the structured payload. If user loses connectivity before DOS, the UI shows a toast "Saved locally — reconnect to finish". On reconnect, reconcile() completes and the message becomes committed and webhooks fire exactly once.

Observability and billing implications
- Each DOS emission, reconcile call, and tool-call receipt is recorded in telemetry. DOS creation cost is negligible and amortized into generation cost. Reconcile endpoints are priced as metadata reads for hosted customers; Dedicated customers may opt for a higher retention TTL.
- Telemetry fields: dos_token, response_id, model_version, token_count_at_seal, tool_call_count, reconcile_latency, reconcile_result_code.

Security and privacy
- DOS tokens are opaque by default. Enterprise customers can enable signed DOS tokens (HMAC) that prove the server produced a particular seal (useful for audit trails).
- Tool-call ledgers store minimal PII; integrations with sensitive outputs are flagged for restricted retention.

Compatibility and migration plan
- Backwards compatible: clients that ignore seals will continue to receive streaming partial_text frames; they will not get reconciliation guarantees but behavior remains unchanged. Servers will emit seals gradually; we will run a soft rollout that enables DOS for a subset of requests (flag-based).
- SDK rollout: ship client helpers (node, python, go, mobile) that implement reconcilers and persistence shims. Start with node and python in alpha, mobile SDKs in beta.

Implementation approach and risks
- Server: add seal generation step to response composer; compute digest with canonicalization rules. Store minimal ledger entries for tool calls keyed by idempotency_key. Risk: increased write load for tool-call ledger—mitigate by TTL, batched writes, and dedicated write paths for Dedicated customers.
- SDK: persistence and reconciliation complexity. Risk of different canonicalization across SDKs—mitigate with shared proto canonicalizer library and integration tests.
- Non-reproducible outputs: some models' sampling may prevent reproducibility; reconcile will surface provenance and we will provide a deterministic-mode flag for customers who require strict reproducibility (may use beam/deterministic decoding).

Launch plan and success metrics
- Alpha (6 weeks): node/python SDK, server emits DOS for 10% of streaming responses, reconcile endpoint read-only.
- Beta (12 weeks): mobile SDKs, signed DOS for enterprise customers, OTS ledger retention increased for paying tiers.
- GA (Q2): full rollout, telemetry dashboards, SLA around reconcile latency (<200ms for typical lookups).

Key metrics to track
- Reconcile success rate (% of reconcilable DOS without duplicate tool calls)
- Average reconcile latency
- Duplicate-execution incidents (per 1k tool calls)
- SDK adoption: % of active clients calling reconcile() within 24h of DOS emission

Open questions and tradeoffs
- TTL for tool-call ledger vs customer need for long-term auditability (Dedicated/private should allow config).
- How to represent complex merges when later DOS updates overwrite structured fragments—need a clear merge algebra.
- Should DOS be per-turn or per-structured-commit? (Per-commit is more explicit but increases seal churn.)

Next steps
- Sync with serving-runtime to validate cost of digest calculation and storage pattern (action: Arjun)
- Prototype node SDK reconcile helper and a small mobile glue layer (action: Lena)
- Draft canonicalization rules and unit tests for deterministic digest (action: Tomás)
- Add JIRA epic to track telemetry fields and dashboard work (action: Priya)

Appendix: quick glossary
- DOS (Deterministic Output Seal): compact commitment token representing canonicalized output prefix and tool intents.
- OTS (Offline Tool Sync): reconciliation layer/read API that returns authoritative tool-call outcomes and structured outputs associated with a DOS.
- idempotency_key: derived key used to deduplicate tool invocations across reconnects.

End of draft.
